Application versions supplied as distribution packages, annotated above their ARG. The datasource builds an index URL out of the registryUrl rather than fetching it, so the branch and component belong in the annotation beside the base image they follow.
Tool versions pinned in a workflow, annotated above their env value

description: local>kanso-labs/.github:renovate-config is the organization's shared Renovate preset, holding the settings that have to hold in every kanso-labs repository. It is listed last because a later preset wins a conflict with an earlier one: moved ahead of config:recommended it would be overridden by the very preset it exists to correct. This file is merged over the runner's config.js rather than inheriting from it, so extending the preset here is what carries an organization-wide setting into this repository at all. See the README in kanso-labs/.github.

packageRules.description: Plex tags carry a per-build commit hash, and docker versioning treats everything after the first dash as a compatibility suffix it will not cross. Every release mints a fresh hash, so no newer tag is ever compatible and no update was ever offered. Parsing the four numeric parts and declaring no compatibility group is what lets the build number order the tags.

base-python tags name a Python and an Alpine release, as in 3.14-alpine3.24, and docker versioning reads everything after the dash as a compatibility suffix it will not cross, so Bazarr sat on Alpine 3.22 after 3.24 shipped and no update was ever offered. Reading the two as one version lets Renovate follow both: a new Python minor arrives as a minor, a new Alpine as a patch. The dated rebuilds, such as 3.14-alpine3.24-2026.10.0, do not match and are never offered, so the floating tag, which Home Assistant keeps rebuilding, stays what is pinned.

Radarr, Sonarr, Prowlarr and s6-overlay publish four-part versions such as 2.6.5.5623, which are not valid semver. semver-coerced, the default versioning, therefore judges every one of them unstable, the pin included, and from an unstable pin it offers only releases sharing its major, minor and patch. None of those coerces to anything greater, so no update was ever offered and nothing was logged. Matching the pin's shape rather than a list of names catches the next application that versions this way, and GitHub's prerelease flag still keeps the develop builds out.

Annotated versions the shared ^v(?<version>.*)$ reads wrongly. Renovate writes back what extractVersion extracts, and the Immich images are written as the tag they name, v and all, so stripping the v would bump them to a tag that does not exist. VectorChord's release tags, Valkey's image tags and the PyPI versions of certbot and cryptography carry no v at all, and a release the shared pattern cannot match is dropped rather than offered, so they would never have been updated. These keep their versions whole.

UnRAR has no repository or registry to ask, so the rarlab datasource reads RARLAB's download page, and every link on it comes back as a candidate version. This keeps the version out of the source tarball's name, unrarsrc-7.3.1.tar.gz, and drops every other link, in place of the shared ^v(?<version>.*)$, which none of them would match. The page links RARLAB's betas too, under names that look exactly like a release: unrarsrc-7.3.1 is UnRAR 7.30 beta 1. Nothing in the name tells them apart, so no UnRAR update merges on its own, and Bazarr's build reads RARVER_BETA in the tarball's version.hpp and fails on a beta. allowedVersions keeps 7.3.1 from being proposed again once Bazarr has gone back from it, which Renovate would otherwise do at once, whatever recreateWhen says, because the pull request that brought it in was merged rather than closed. Take it out once RARLAB links a later tarball.

Images pinned by the annotation above their ARG, which is what lets one version serve every stage built from it. The Dockerfile manager resolves that ARG inside FROM as well and would offer a second update for the same line, and for the OpenVINO stage one it cannot apply at all, since v3.2.4-openvino appears nowhere literally. The annotation is the one source.
The upper bound of VECTORCHORD_VERSION_RANGE in Immich's server/src/constants.ts. Immich will not start against a VectorChord outside it, so raise this when Immich does.
The pgvector versions Immich documents VectorChord as known to work with, at least 0.7 and below 0.9. Raise this when Immich does.
The Valkey major Immich's own compose file runs. Raise this when upstream does.

Avahi Publisher, NAT Gateway and qBittorrent pin Alpine packages to an exact revision from the index branch their annotation names, so the base image's next Alpine release fails their build until someone moves that branch and picks the versions again. Grouped on their own, that failure holds back only these three, rather than every application on a Home Assistant base image. It follows the group above, so it wins for these files.
packageRules.groupName: Home Assistant Base Images with Alpine package pins

packageRules.description: Home Assistant rebuilds its base images under the same tag, with whatever security fixes their distribution has shipped since. A tag alone changes nothing in this repository when that happens, and an application publishes a version only once, so the rebuild reached installs only when the application happened to release for some other reason. Pinned by digest, each rebuild is a pull request in the groups above, typed deps, so every application on that base releases a patch carrying it.

A digest update is a rebuild of the same base release, which the shared preset's automerge for minors and patches does not cover. It merges once the required checks pass, as a patch would. Renovate types the first pin of a digest as pinDigest rather than digest, and it merges the same way, so a base image that arrives without a digest is pinned without waiting for a person.

The application versions users actually see, typed fix so that they release under Bug Fixes rather than Dependencies. That is the patch: the two rules below retype a minor as feat and a major as feat!, so each release takes the step upstream took. They find these applications by the fix this rule gives them, so this list is the only one to keep, and it has to stay above them.

An application's minor release is a minor release of ours. Matching on the type the rule above gave rather than restating its list works because Renovate checks each rule against the config every earlier rule has already applied.

An application's major release is a major release of ours. The ! is what makes release-please read a breaking change, and it reaches the pull request title intact. Majors do not automerge, so each one waits for a person.

Below 1.0 an upstream's minor release is its breaking one, and the shared preset automerges minors. That is how Flight Finder 0.16.0, which replaced its sign-in, was merged and released with nobody having read its notes. So a minor of an application still below 1.0 waits for a person, as a major does, while its patches still automerge. It finds the applications by the feat the minor rule above gave them, and it follows the preset's automerge rule, as every rule in this file does, so it wins.

Authentik numbers its releases by date, so Renovate reads a feature release such as 2026.8 to 2026.11 as a minor, although upstream treats each one as a major and opens its notes with breaking changes. Its bumps also arrive without those notes. So a feature release waits for a person, as a major does. It follows the preset's automerge rule, as every rule in this file does, so it wins. Patches still automerge while no feature release is waiting, since Renovate folds them into the minor while one is. Merge each one before the next ships: Authentik will not migrate a database more than one feature release old, and a waiting pull request moves to the newest release when another lands, which would skip one.

Immich expects its server and its machine learning to be the same version, so a new release moves both applications in one pull request. That pull request releases both, the one intended exception to one application per pull request.

n8n's lockfile decides every package its image installs, and Renovate refreshes it with every n8n bump, so the two move together. Daily lock file maintenance would move it on its own instead, in a pull request typed chore, which changes the image and releases nothing. The site's lockfile is left to that maintenance, since nothing ships from it.

These images carry no org.opencontainers.image.source label, so Renovate finds no repository for them and their bumps arrive without upstream's release notes. Naming the repository each one's DOCS.md credits is what lets it look them up.
As above, for Flight Finder.
